description: Cluster 1: Digital platforms, big data, and circular economy in Ecommerce. This cluster has seven publications with 97 citations and an average of 13.86 citations per article and a total link strength (TLS) of 26. About 71% of the publications were published in 2023, which shows the emerging nature of this cluster. The first publication was done in 2016 (Thiyagarajan and Ali, 2016). The interconnection between digital platforms and physical sustainability in e-commerce is the main issue of this cluster, and the focus is on packaging and the implementation of the circular economy. Ram et al. (2025) argue that the concern for the environment is more influential than the monetary rewards to consumers in the emerging markets. Online reviews generate big data analytics that are used to understand customer environmental concerns. Mariani and Borghi (2023) show that in the case of environmentally protective reviews, product ratings are improved, whereas Na et al. (2024) employ sentiment analysis and transfer learning to measure consumer perception of energy-efficient products. In general, this cluster demonstrates the intersection of the concept of digital technologies, such as Big Data and AI, and green consumer behavior, and offers practical options, like the idea of the circular economy as a model of e-commerce packaging.

Cluster 2: Theoretical foundations of sharing economy and collaborative consumption. Six publications in this cluster generate 339 citations, with an average of 56.5 citations per paper, which is the greatest number of citations per paper on average within all the clusters. The total link strength (TLS) is 26. Piscicelli et al. (2015) present the original work, having 290 citations and being at the center of the cluster. Even though the cluster emerged in 2015, research is still ongoing up to 2025. The cluster is dedicated to the creation of theoretical frameworks of collaborative consumption in the context of the sharing economy, and specifically to the significance of individual values to sharing behavior. Piscicelli et al. (2015) utilize the value framework provided by Schwartz to explain the case of a lending system in the United Kingdom. Further research advances the research question about obstacles and motivation of the sharing economy. Bhalla (2023) adds a socio-psychological approach to the study of how trust can be used to encourage collaborative consumption. Overall, Cluster 2 provides the theoretical foundation of the field, shifting the focus from abstract conceptualization of sharing values to the analysis of practical facilitators and barriers to collaborative consumption. It serves as a conceptual anchor to other subsequent clusters, particularly those that are concerned with value measurement and consumer behavior.

Cluster 3: behavioral interventions and nudging in online food consumption. Five publications in this little yet very recent cluster have a cumulative total number of 29 citations, and the average number of citations per paper was 5.8; the total link strength (TLS) of the cluster is 19. They were all published in 2024, and it was an innovative focus. The cluster focuses on the implementation of behavioral economics and the use of direct interventions in the e-commerce environment to facilitate sustainable decisions, especially for products such as food. Examples of nudges used by Katare and Zhao (2024) include carbon-footprint labels and product categorization in online shopping, which, in turn, leads to a 2537% increase in the choice of plant-based foods. Najafabadiha et al. (2025) use educational videos and eye-tracking technology, which prove effective in raising attention to and prioritization of green products. The cluster represents a transition from observational research to solution design, which involves powerful interventional approaches, including neuromarketing and behavioral experiments. It represents both a methodological innovation and an expansion of experimental methods of research on sustainable consumption.

Cluster 4: importance of sustainability attributes in purchase decisions (fashion industry). This cluster has five publications with a cumulative 198 citations, an average of 39.6 citations per publication, and a TLS of 21. The majority of the papers were written in 2021, with additional studies in 2022 and 2023, forming a short but effective research wave. It is also concentrated on the online fashion market, where the question is whether sustainability has a significant impact on buying behavior. With 95 citations, Rausch et al. (2021) utilize best-worst scaling and discover that consumers are ready to choose vital sustainable qualities, including longevity and fair pay, instead of a 20 per cent discount. Feuβ et al. (2022) examine the interaction effect between eco-labels and price in field research. Li et al. (2023) present new technologies in e-commerce that compare the contribution of visual information to the development of sustainable purchasing attitudes with voice assistants and show that the impact is contingent on the environmental knowledge of consumers. This cluster indicates that sustainability is now a feasible product quality in the fashion world. It can also have a direct impact on purchase behavior and, in fact, may surpass financial incentives rather than being a secondary factor. Voice assistant research is another area that is opening up as shopping platforms become more auditory, making it difficult to communicate sustainability information.

Cluster 5: Motivation and adoption of the sharing economy through self-determination theory. This cluster comprises five publications with a total of 102 citations, averaging 20.4 citations per paper, and a TLS of 45, the highest in the network. Most papers were published in 2022, with others from 2020 to 2023, showing strong academic concentration and connectivity. The cluster clarifies motivations for participating in the sharing economy using Self-Determination Theory (SDT). Studies differentiate intrinsic motivations, such as enjoyment and a sense of belonging, from extrinsic motivations, including economic benefits and reputation. Oliveira et al. (2022) apply SDT to explain continued usage intentions and post-adoption behavior. Kaushal and Prashar (2022), in emerging markets like India, demonstrate that both intrinsic motivations and extrinsic economic benefits are strong determinants. Specific applications in bike-sharing are also discussed (Da Silveira et al., 2022). This cluster represents the maturity phase of sharing economy research, moving from definitions and value-focused studies (Cluster 2) to explaining behavioral mechanisms through a robust psychological theory. The application of SDT clarifies why users participate and informs the design of interventions to encourage more sustainable behaviors within the sharing economy.

Cluster 6 (Teal): theoretical models (TPB) and psychological factors in contemporary shopping. This cluster comprises five publications with a total of 125 citations, averaging 25 citations per paper, and a total link strength (TLS) of 38. The publications span from 2018 to 2025 and focus on extending classical behavioral models in the context of modern e-commerce. Yang et al. (2018) applied the extended Theory of Planned Behavior (TPB) during the Double-11 festival, finding that festive atmosphere can weaken sustainable consumption intentions, contrary to expectations. Rao et al. (2021) analyzed the impact of e-commerce supply chains on environmental sustainability, while Doan et al. (2025) explored new topics, showing that cashless payment can promote impulse buying, but this effect may be moderated by mindfulness. This cluster demonstrates how behavioral theories such as TPB are being adapted to emerging contexts, including FinTech and digital payments. New phenomena, such as impulse buying and overconsumption, require classical models to incorporate self-regulatory psychological structures, reflecting the intersection of e-commerce research, consumer psychology, and sustainability.

Cluster 7 (Orange): specialized applications – sharing economy and Willingness to Pay for Premium (WTPP). The smallest cluster comprises three publications with a total of 33 citations, averaging 11 citations per paper, and a TLS of 7.1. The publications appear between 2022 and 2023. This cluster focuses on specialized topics related to sustainability and the sharing economy. Bo and Yang (2022) used randomized auction experiments to measure WTPP for agricultural products, showing that regional branding attracts higher and more sustainable WTPP than corporate branding. Mattia et al. (2022) analyzed the intentions of first-time users of peer-to-peer ride-sharing services. P´erez-P´erez et al. (2023) expanded the analysis of the sharing economy to a macro perspective, linking it to the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). This cluster highlights high methodological experimentation, applying major theoretical frameworks such as WTPP and sharing economy concepts in specific contexts, while also bridging connections with other clusters in the research network. Overall, the bibliographic analysis delineates a detailed knowledge map of green consumer behavior in e-commerce. The seven-cluster structure illustrates a rapidly developing field, transitioning from classical psychological theories to an interdisciplinary domain enriched by advanced technologies. The field actively integrates tools from computer science (AI, Big Data), experimental psychology (neuromarketing, eye-tracking), and behavioral economics (nudging, auction experiments) to address one of the most pressing challenges of the digital era: reconciling the convenience of e-commerce with the urgent global need for sustainability
